passages.happening:
“In the days when the judges ruled, there was a famine in the land. And a certain man from Bethlehem in Judah, with his wife and two sons, went to reside in the land of Moab” (verse 1).

The man is Elimelech, his wife is Naomi, and their sons are Mahlon and Chilion. They are Ephrathites from Bethlehem, and they settle in Moab (verse 2).

Elimelech dies, and Naomi is left with her two sons (verse 3). They marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. After about ten years both sons die too, ‘and Naomi was left without her two sons and without her husband’ (verses 4-5).
passages.hearers:
The first words set the story in a dark time, the days of the judges, when Israel had no king and everyone did what was right in his own eyes. The book of Judges told those years through wars and leaders. Ruth tells them through one family.

Bethlehem lay in the hill country of Judah, about six miles south of Jerusalem. Its name means house of bread. A famine in the house of bread is the first irony of the book. Famines were a constant danger in a land that lived by seasonal rain, and they drove people to look for food elsewhere, as they had driven Abraham, Isaac and the sons of Jacob.

Moab lay east of the Dead Sea, on a high plateau of grain fields and pasture, several days' walk from Bethlehem. Relations between Israel and Moab were strained. Israel remembered that Moab's king had hired Balaam to curse it, that Moabite women had drawn Israelites into the worship of Baal of Peor, and that in the days of Ehud a king of Moab had ruled over Israel for eighteen years. The law barred Moabites from the assembly of the LORD. An Israelite family settling in Moab, and sons marrying Moabite women, would have raised questions for a first hearer.

Then the losses pile up in a few short verses. In that world a widow without a husband or sons usually had no land, no income and no one to speak for her in law. Naomi is left with nothing but two daughters-in-law from a foreign land.
passages.later:
Famine had driven Israel's fathers from the land before: “Now there was a famine in the land. So Abram went down to Egypt to live there for a while because the famine was severe” (Genesis 12:10).

The law's word about Moab stands behind the whole story: “No Ammonite or Moabite or any of their descendants may enter the assembly of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 23:3).
passages.hard:
Was Elimelech wrong to go to Moab, and were his sons wrong to marry Moabite women? Were their deaths a punishment?

The text does not say so. Some readers, especially in Jewish tradition, have seen the deaths as judgment for leaving the promised land and marrying foreign women, pointing to the law about Moab and to the warning against marrying the peoples of the land.

Others notice that the narrator passes no such judgment, that famine was a good reason to look for food elsewhere, as Abraham and Jacob did, and that the warning in Deuteronomy 7 names the peoples of Canaan, not Moab. The rest of the book shows a Moabite woman welcomed by Israel's God and people and becoming the great-grandmother of David. That suggests the book's concern is not to condemn these choices but to show God's grace working through and beyond them.

Readers disagree on how much blame to give, and the text leaves the question open. It gives no one cause to read a death in their own family as God's sentence on them.
passages.asks: Naomi lost her husband and both sons in a foreign land. Ask how you speak of losses like hers, whether you reach first for a reason or first for the person. And if you are carrying a loss of your own, ask whether you have let anyone sit with you in it.

passages.happening:
Naomi hears that the LORD has come to the help of his people by giving them food, and she sets out for home with her two daughters-in-law (verses 6-7).

On the road she stops them. “Go back, each of you to your mother’s home. May the LORD show you loving devotion, as you have shown to your dead and to me” (verse 8). She prays that each will find rest in the home of a new husband, and kisses them, and they weep aloud and say they will go with her (verses 9-10).

Naomi presses them. She has no more sons to give them as husbands, and even if she did, would they wait for them to grow up? She says, “it grieves me very much for your sakes that the hand of the LORD has gone out against me” (verse 13). They weep again. Orpah kisses her mother-in-law goodbye, ‘but Ruth clung to her’ (verse 14).

Naomi tells Ruth to follow Orpah back to her people and her gods (verse 15). Ruth answers: “Do not urge me to leave you or to turn from following you. For wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you live, I will live; your people will be my people, and your God will be my God” (verse 16). “Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me” (verse 17). When Naomi sees that Ruth is determined, she says no more (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
This is one of only two places in the book where the narrator says plainly that the LORD acted: he ‘had attended to His people by providing them with food’ (verse 6).

The chapter turns on one Hebrew word, to return or turn back, which comes again and again. Naomi returns to Judah. She urges her daughters-in-law to return to their mothers' homes. Orpah returns to her people and her gods. Ruth refuses to turn back, and so she ‘returns’ to a land she has never lived in. The same verb is used by the prophets for turning back to God.

Naomi's advice is practical. Young widows could remarry in Moab, where they had families. A Moabite widow in Judah would have little chance. Her words about sons in her womb point to the custom by which a dead man's brother married his widow to give him an heir, and she says how impossible that is for her. Orpah does what Naomi asks, and the book never blames her.

Ruth's words are more than devotion. In that world a people and its god belonged together. To change peoples was to change gods. She binds herself to Naomi's people, to Naomi's God, the LORD, and even to Naomi's grave, which meant giving up her own family's burial place forever. She seals it with an oath in the LORD's name. It is a covenant promise.

‘Clung’ is the word used in Genesis of a man holding fast to his wife, and in Deuteronomy of Israel holding fast to the LORD. Ruth's words are often read at weddings. In the story they are spoken by a widow to her widowed mother-in-law, with nothing to gain.
passages.later:
The word for Ruth's clinging is the word of the first marriage: “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife” (Genesis 2:24). And it is the word of Israel's loyalty to God: “You are to fear the LORD your God and serve Him. Hold fast to Him” (Deuteronomy 10:20).

Matthew remembers her in the family line of Jesus: “Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth” (Matthew 1:5).
passages.asks: Orpah went home, and Ruth stayed, and the book honors both. Ask whom you have bound yourself to, not because it pays but because love keeps faith. And hear Ruth's words again. Ask what it would mean for you to say to God, ‘your God will be my God’, and to mean the grave as well as the road.

passages.happening:
The two women walk on until they come to Bethlehem. The whole town is stirred, and the women ask, “Can this be Naomi?” (verse 19).

“Do not call me Naomi,” she replied. “Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me. I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty” (verses 20-21). Why call her Naomi, she asks, when the LORD has testified against her and the Almighty has afflicted her?

“So Naomi returned from the land of Moab with her daughter-in-law Ruth the Moabitess. And they arrived in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Naomi means pleasant. Mara means bitter. She asks the town to call her by her grief.

She uses the name the Almighty twice. It is a name for God linked with his power in the stories of Abraham and in Job. Naomi still believes in that power. She feels it has been turned against her.

‘I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty.’ This is the book's starting point. The rest of the story answers it, not with an argument but with events. In chapter 3 Boaz will send Ruth home with barley so that she does not return ‘empty-handed’, the same word, and in chapter 4 the women will place a child in Naomi's lap.

Notice too what Naomi does not say. She speaks of coming back empty, with Ruth standing beside her. The reader can already see what Naomi cannot yet see.

The last verse gives two quiet signs of hope. Ruth is with her, and they arrive at the beginning of the barley harvest, in spring, around April. The famine that began the story is over.
passages.later: The Bible gives grief like Naomi's its own words. Job said, “The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away” (Job 1:21), and a psalm cries, “My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?” (Psalm 22:1). Naomi's complaint stands in that company.
passages.hard:
Naomi says the Almighty has dealt bitterly with her and has testified against her. Is it wrong to speak to God, or about God, like that?

The book does not rebuke her. It does not argue with her grief or hurry her out of it. It answers her slowly, through what happens next. The Bible keeps many such words, in Job and in the psalms of lament, and it treats honest grief as a way of speaking to God, not a failure of faith.

If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, or you feel you do not want to go on, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. You do not have to carry it alone. If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Naomi told the town to call her bitter, and the Bible let her say it. Ask whether you have ever hidden your grief from God because it sounded too harsh, and what it would mean to say it to him plainly. And look at who is standing beside Naomi as she speaks. Ask who is standing beside you that you have not yet seen.
